expert_quote: Unfortunately, that had to do with the fact that this AI machine learning solution [required] a certain degree of collaboration between the sales recruiters. expert_quote: In the end, I think only the code got saved on that on that storage somewhere, but also not fully implemented unfortunately.
rationale: This outcome describes a classic form of integration debt. The AI component (code) is developed but becomes a stranded asset—'saved on storage'—because it fails to be integrated into the live organizational system and processes, likely due to the socio-cultural frictions described earlier.

expert_quote: But with machine learning AI there's this little extra abstraction layer which is just very hard for... non... core data experts to to fully appreciate. So I think that requires even more alignment.
rationale: The 'extra abstraction layer' creates a cognitive gap that slows down communication and shared understanding between technical (AI-time) and business (organizational-time) teams. Person 2 identifies this as a primary reason for requiring 'even more alignment,' which is a direct consequence of the clash between the complex, fast-evolving logic of AI and the slower, sequential pace of organizational learning and decision-making.

expert_quote: Spent a little bit less time behind the laptop and more times in in teams and in reality to to really, yeah, keep everyone involved because then the acceptance rate at the end will be much higher although the technical progress will be a little bit slower.
rationale: Here, Person 2 explicitly prescribes a trade-off: sacrificing speed of technical development ('AI time') to invest in slower, human-centric alignment activities ('organizational time') to ensure ultimate adoption. This advice is a direct managerial response to the inherent temporal misalignment between AI development cycles and the human/organizational change cycle.
